4677.t: From Lydian [script needed] (*luwdja, “Luwia”), where the Lydians came to live after being driven away by the Phrygians. Here the -d- is result of affrication of proto-Luwian *-j-.

4650.t: Derived from the root of ὄναρ (ónăr) with a suffix *-yos.Cognate with Old Armenian անուրջ (anurǰ) and Albanian ëndërr.

4686.t: From σάμος (sắmos, “seaside hill; dune; height”), from Phoenician 𐤔𐤌𐤀 (sama, “high”).

4687.t: Possibly from τίτο (títo, “sun, day”), which is an Anatolian loan-word, or from τιταίνω (titaínō, “to stretch, to extend”), from τείνω (teínō), or from τίσις (tísis, “retribution”), from τίνω (tínō, “to pay a price as a penalty, expiate”), respectively, as…

4664.t: From a *suh₂-, which, according to the linguist Jay Jasonoff, is a metathesized form from the zero-grade of the root which is to be reconstructed as Proto-Indo-European *sh₂ew- (“to pour, scatter, rain”).

4665.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *sew-? Proto-Indo-European *sewH-? Proto-Indo-European *suH- Proto-Hellenic *hūs Ancient Greek ὗς Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *hūs, from Proto-Indo-European *suH- (“swine”).

4694.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewg- (“to lighten up”), which is likely a semantic extension of *h₂ewg- in the usual "to increase" sense.

4638.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₃m̥bʰ-l̥- (“navel”), from *h₃nebʰ- (“navel, center”). Cognates include Sanskrit नभ्य (nábhya), Latin umbilīcus, and Old English nafola (English navel).

4649.t: Traditionally connected to Sanskrit अभ्र (abhrá), Latin imber, and Old Armenian ամբ (amb), but formal derivation from Proto-Indo-European *n̥bʰrós presents several problems. *n̥, *bʰ would be expected to yield α, φ (ă, ph), although Miller's law would…

4689.t: Contracted from *ἀεικεία (*aeikeíā), from ἀ- (ă-, “not”) + εἰκός (eikós, “reasonable, fair”) + -εία (-eíā, abstract noun suffix).

4699.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂ews- Proto-Indo-European *-r Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewsér Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwsr̥h₂ Proto-Hellenic *auhrā Ancient Greek αὔρα From Proto-Hellenic *auhrā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwsr̥h₂…

4617.t: From the root of ἔργον (érgon, “work”) + -της (-tēs, masculine agentive suffix).

4651.t: From the root of ὑμεῖς (hūmeîs, “you”, plural) + -τερος (-teros, contrastive adjective suffix).

4670.t: Of unclear origin. Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *werb- (“to bend, turn”), and compared with Latin verber (“lash, whip”), Proto-Germanic *warpą (“warp”), but this is phonetically impossible.

4635.t: A loanword of unclear source, but possibly Egyptian in origin. Compare Biblical Hebrew יָשְׁפֵה (yāšəfēh, “jasper”), Amarna Akkadian 𒉌𒌓𒅀𒀸𒁍 (/⁠yašpû⁠/, “name of a stone”) (whence Classical Syriac ܝܫܦܐ (jaʃpɑ(ʔ), “jasper”)).

4645.t: From ὅμιλος (hómīlos, “a crowd or gathering of people”) + -ία (-ĭ́ā).

4634.t: From Proto-Hellenic *wīrāks, from Proto-Indo-European *wiHrós (“man”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *weyh₁- (“to chase, pursue”), with possible folk-etymological influence by ἱερός (hĭerós, “holy, divine”).

4633.t: ἱκνέομαι (hĭknéomai, “to come”) + -της (-tēs, “-er”, masculine agent-noun suffix): literally, “comer”.

4655.t: From ὑπο- (hupo-, “hypo-, under-”) + ἴσχω (ískhō, “to keep”), apparently modified under the influence of ἀρνέομαι (arnéomai, “to deny, refuse”).

4643.t: From a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi (“on”); related to ὀπίσω (opísō, “after”) and ὄπισθεν (ópisthen, “in the future”).

4640.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₃n̥-né-h₂-ti, from the root *h₃neh₂- (“to enjoy”). Cognate with Proto-Germanic *unnaną.
